lines: A team picks a well-known orchestrator for one reason: everyone else they know already uses it.
A year later, they're spending more engineer time keeping that system's own scheduler and database healthy than they ever spent writing the actual pipelines.
A much lighter, fully managed option would have fit their actual workload for a fraction of that ongoing cost.
The tool wasn't wrong in general. It was wrong for this specific job.
So what should actually decide a choice like that? Four separate questions, not one gut feeling.
Does the workload react to data showing up, or does it just run on a schedule.
How much ongoing care does running the system yourself demand, versus letting someone else run it.
And two more worth naming here: how rich is its surrounding ecosystem, and how hard would it be to walk away from later.
Before naming the answer, think about the team from the very start of this topic.
Their workload runs quickly, happens constantly, and needs no custom code written specifically for it.
None of those traits particularly favor the tool they picked.
Which of the four questions actually explains why they picked it anyway?
steps.answer: None of them, really. They optimized for familiarity -- the tool they already knew how to run -- rather than for how well it actually fit this particular job.

lines: One well-known cloud provider offers two distinct flavors of a fully managed, serverless workflow tool, sourced directly from their own documentation.
One flavor is built to run for a very long time, up to a full year, and guarantees each step happens exactly once.
The other flavor is built to finish quickly, within minutes, and only guarantees each step happens at least once, possibly more.
Same underlying product name. Two genuinely different promises, priced in two completely different ways.
steps.takeaway: A serverless state machine isn't one tool with two modes. It's two different trade-offs wearing the same name.

lines: Worth pausing on this before it's shown.
An earlier topic in this chapter covered a task graph that could expand itself to match data discovered while it ran.
Does this cloud provider's own serverless workflow tool have anything built specifically for that same shape of problem?
Think about whether fan-out like that has to be hand-rolled, or whether it comes as a real, managed feature.
steps.answer: It comes as a real, dedicated feature. Large-scale fan-out isn't something you have to build yourself here -- it's offered as a first-class, managed primitive.

lines: Here's that exact feature, sourced directly rather than just described.
By default, it can run an enormous number of these child pieces of work in parallel -- on the order of ten thousand at once.
Each one of those child pieces keeps its own separate history, entirely apart from the parent that launched it.
That separation is deliberate, not incidental.
steps.takeaway: A managed fan-out primitive isn't a bigger loop. It gives every child its own history, by design.

lines: Worth naming the rest of this field quickly, each sourced from its own documentation.
Two more Python-native tools embrace genuinely dynamic flows the same spirit as before. One well-known alternative writes everything declaratively in plain structured text instead of code.
One system is named and sourced from its own published write-up, since it isn't something you can simply install and run yourself.
And a well-known cloud data platform's own orchestration feature was recently given a brand new name as part of a bigger product announcement.
Pulling it all together now.

Four questions decide a real choice here, not one single favorite tool: how data-aware it needs to be, how much ongoing care it demands, how rich its ecosystem is, and how hard it'd be to leave later.
The team from the very start of this topic optimized for none of those four questions.
They optimized for what they already happened to know.
steps.takeaway: There is no single best orchestrator. There is only the tool that fits a workload on all four axes.

lines: One more scenario to test this against.
A different workload this time: it finishes quickly, happens extremely often, and needs no custom code written specifically for it.
Does that same four-question approach still point toward the exact tool the first team chose?
Or does it point somewhere else entirely, once the job's actual shape is taken seriously?
steps.answer: It points somewhere else. This workload's shape matches the quick, high-volume flavor of serverless workflow almost exactly -- the four questions don't favor any one tool by habit, only by fit.
